transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-24
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz, Marcus Chen, Priya Rao - Redwood; Sofia Patel, Tom Reyes, Maya Nguyen, Evan Liu - Brightline Retail

Summary (auto): Quick postmortem + ops handoff after Friday's eviction-wave. Focus on preventing fallback amplification and reducing unit cost impact by smarter circuit breakers, cache tuning, and telemetry.

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: okay, thanks everyone for joining, we'll try to keep this tight. Marcus and I will run through the backfill of the postmortem and then go into the mitigation playbook. Sofia, you said you'd share the traffic profile up-front?
[00:14] Sofia Patel: yeah sorry, I pulled a couple samples, Evan sent over the long tail distribution this morning but, um, TL;DR we had a spike that shifted 3x on tail length, so KV cache got churned.
[00:29] Marcus Chen: right, our hypothesis is prefix cache fragmentation + a couple of cold starts that caused hot keys to miss, leading to upstream timeouts and then the circuit breaker feeding more requests to the fallback model which is heavy and slow.
[00:45] Tom Reyes: can I jump in? we also saw some eviction events on our end when disk-backed shard got pressure, so I think it's both sides—the client and the runtime.
[00:58] Lena Ortiz: good point. quick question — when you say eviction events, are those at the Redis layer or at your local application cache?
[01:08] Tom Reyes: mostly Redis, but the application layer had some bursty load causing bigger item churn. Some keys were TTLed aggressively by our app logic, probably a config change that rolled out Thursday.
[01:22] Maya Nguyen: and we have an open retrier that kept retrying 4xx on certain paths, which amplified ingress — we fixed the retrier after the fact.
[01:34] Marcus Chen: thanks — that explains why the sequence length increased for a subset of requests, so runtime kernel selection saw a skew and queued longer. The continuous-batching algorithm then tried to pack tokens and that increased latency variance.
[01:50] Evan Liu: the long lived keys sample shows about 12% of keys account for 60% of hits but the churned set replaced those quickly during the spike, so the KV cache wasn't able to warm.
[02:05] Lena Ortiz: ok let's move to concrete mitigations. Marcus?
[02:10] Marcus Chen: proposed mitigations: 1) adjust circuit-breaker thresholds to be latency-and-error aware (not just token-level), 2) add an aggressive short-term cold-key bypass so we don't try heavy fallback on brand-new prefixes, 3) KV cache TTL smoothing and sticky partitions for hot keys, 4) optional dedicated buffer capacity for short burst absorption.
[02:35] Tom Reyes: what does "cold-key bypass" mean in practice? will requests be dropped?
[02:42] Marcus Chen: no, not dropped: lightweight path — we serve a cheaper/quantized variant for cold prefixes for first N requests, then promote if hot. It's like a warmup policy. We can configure promotion thresholds.
[02:54] Maya Nguyen: that sounds promising. but we need guarantees — if promotion lags we might get more inconsistency.
[03:02] Priya Rao: we can couple promotion with telemetry so ops see a promotion lag metric. We'll include a dashboard for that.
[03:10] Sofia Patel: also need to see cost delta, if we switch to quantized variant for a subset will that change per-token billing?
[03:18] Lena Ortiz: billing won't change for hosted model variants unless you choose a different model SKU; however, using quantized variants or dedicated buffer has different unit economics — we'll put numbers in the pricing sheet. I'll send a delta later today.
[03:34] Marcus Chen: about circuit breakers — sample policy: error-rate > 5% OR p95 latency > 800ms AND sustained for 12s triggers a fast-fail for the heavy fallback for 30s with exponential backoff. We can tune the windows.
[03:50] Tom Reyes: 12 seconds is pretty short. what about transient infra jitter?
[03:56] Marcus Chen: fair — we can use a sliding window with 3-of-5 samples and require a minimum absolute count to avoid flapping on small samples.
[04:08] Evan Liu: do we have the ability to route to a less-capable model automatically? we could fall back to a smaller quantized model that meets latency SLO.
[04:16] Marcus Chen: yes — Redwoods runtime supports model variants and automatic fallback routing by policy. We can pin to models per route and have auto-fallback to a cheaper model when circuit opens.
[04:27] Lena Ortiz: note for procurement — Dedicated buffer buys are a good runway to avoid bursting into fallback. Lena: (laughs) that's me — procurement question will be in the follow-up.
[04:34] Sofia Patel: on timeline, we need something less than a week; the execs want a clear action plan by next Friday.
[04:41] Priya Rao: we can commit to delivering the runbook and config patch by EOD 9/30, which gives time for testing.
[04:49] Sofia Patel: that's ok as long as we run the stress test before that and see data.
[04:54] Marcus Chen: propose stress test 9/29 at 02:00 PT (low traffic) — Tom will confirm the exact window. We'll replay a scaled up traffic trace with longer tails.
[05:06] Tom Reyes: I'll coordinate with infra and confirm by EOD 9/27.
[05:10] Maya Nguyen: during the stress test, we'll want extra instrumentation — sampling of KV hit/miss, cache promotions, model variant switch counts, per-route P95/P99.
[05:21] Marcus Chen: we'll surface those metrics into the Redwood console dashboard; we'll also add an alert rule for promotion lag.
[05:28] Lena Ortiz: question on rollback: if a policy makes things worse we need a fast rollback path. Priya?
[05:33] Priya Rao: runbook will include rollback commands and a playbook checklist; we'll also add a canary window and read-only verification before full rollout.
[05:41] Evan Liu: any recommendations for circuit breaker parameters to start with? we want something conservative to avoid false positive triggers.
[05:48] Marcus Chen: start with p95>900ms OR error-rate>7% sustained for 20s, min 100 samples, then iterate after stress test. We'll send a config diff.
[05:59] Sofia Patel: also we need an incident comms paragraph we can send to customers explaining mitigation steps; ops wants a short blurb.
[06:08] Lena Ortiz: we'll draft a blurb — Priya can own the first draft.
[06:12] Priya Rao: yep I'll send the blurb and Slack templates.
[06:18] (short silence, people reviewing shared doc)
[06:25] Marcus Chen: one more technical note: the runtime's continuous batching can be told to respect route-level max batch size for critical routes; that reduces latency variance at the cost of throughput. Might be useful for checkout routes.
[06:40] Tom Reyes: for checkout we accept slightly higher cost to keep latency tight. We'll mark those routes as critical.
[06:47] Marcus Chen: perfect — create a tag for critical routes and we'll wire circuit and batching policies to that tag.
[06:55] Sofia Patel: ok final recap please?
[07:00] Lena Ortiz: recap: Marcus will deliver policy and config diff (due 9/30), Priya will draft runbook and comms, Tom/Evan will prepare traffic profile and confirm stress-test window by 9/27, Lena will send pricing delta. Stress test target 9/29, review 9/30.
[07:20] Maya Nguyen: thanks everyone — we'll be available for the stress test and want a short dry run before pushing configs to prod.
[07:30] Lena Ortiz: noted. thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites and links to the test harness.

End of transcript. Some speech recognition errors present (e.g., proper nouns and timings).
